1044.title: The breath that won: prana
1044.hook: the senses argue over which of them matters most, and the breath settles it by leaving
1044.carry: prana: the breath is life, and sacred
1044.tomorrow: why do Hindu chants end with peace three times?
1044.howItsDone: Many Hindus begin daily prayer (sandhya) with pranayama, steadying the breath before the mantras; some traditional families offer the first bites of a meal to prana with prāṇāya svāhā; Sanskrit students learn each consonant plain and breathed, sometimes with a hand before the mouth to feel the breath.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-FORTY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the dot underneath: the tongue curled back, and the r that is a vowel, in Kṛṣṇa. Today, the letter h, and the breath inside the holy words.
screen: `SANSKRIT SOUNDS FOR READERS.` · `THE DOT MEANS: CURL THE TONGUE.`

segments.voice: The Chandogya Upanishad tells of a quarrel inside a person. Speech, the eye, the ear and the mind each claim to be the greatest, so they go to their father, Prajapati, the Creator, to judge. He says: the greatest is the one whose leaving leaves the body worst off. Speech leaves for a year. The body lives on, mute. The eye leaves; it lives on, blind. The ear goes, then the mind; still it lives. Then the breath begins to go, and it tears all the others loose, like a strong horse pulling up its tethering pegs.
screen: `SPEECH, EYE, EAR, MIND: WHO IS GREATEST?` → `EACH LEAVES FOR A YEAR.` → `THEN THE BREATH STIRS.`

segments.voice: They all cry out: stay. You are the best of us. That breath is prana, and this little story is one of the Upanishads' ways of saying that breath isn't just air. Prana is the life in you, the power that keeps speech and sight and thought alive. Hindu practice takes that seriously. The daily prayer called sandhya includes pranayama near its start: the breath is steadied before the sacred words are said. Later in the same Upanishad, the first bites of a meal are offered to the breath within, with the words prāṇāya svāhā, to prana, I offer; some traditional families still begin meals that way. And the alphabet itself remembers. Sanskrit grammarians sort consonants by breath. A plain consonant is alpaprana, little breath. One written with an h is mahaprana, great breath. That h isn't a new sound. It's a puff of air. So bh is a b that breathes, as in clubhouse: Bhagavan, the Lord, and bhakti, devotion, both open with it. Dh is a d that breathes, as in roadhouse: dharma lets out a little air before it says anything else. Even atha, now, the first word of the Yoga Sutras, is a t at the teeth and then breath, never the th of thin. Many teachers put it simply: every holy word rides out on prana. To say a name of God with its breath let through is to offer the very thing the whole body, in the story, couldn't live without.
screen: `STAY. YOU ARE THE BEST OF US.` · `BREATH FIRST, THEN THE SACRED WORDS.` · `ALPAPRANA, MAHAPRANA: LITTLE BREATH, GREAT BREATH.` · `BH, DH: LETTERS THAT BREATHE.` · then, large: `EVERY HOLY WORD RIDES ON PRANA.`

segments.voice: Sit the way many begin sandhya: back easy, a few slow breaths, just noticing prana come and go. Then hold your palm near your mouth and say ba, then bha; da, then dha, feeling the great breath land on your hand. If you pray, say one name you pray with, Bhagavan or another, letting every breath letter breathe, as an offering. If not, say dharma slowly and feel the air move.
Bha. A b with great breath, the sound that opens Bhagavan and bhakti: prana, riding out inside a letter.

1045.title: Peace three times: om shanti
1045.hook: a student gives back all he learned, partridges peck it up, and their school asks for peace
1045.carry: shanti three times: within, around, beyond
1045.tomorrow: what did Krishna say about results you can't control?
1045.howItsDone: Teachers and students across India chant saha nāvavatu before study, and countless pujas, readings and gatherings close with om shantih shantih shantih, traditionally explained as peace from three sources of trouble; reciters let the final visarga breathe out softly.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-FORTY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, bha and prana: the breath the body can't live without, riding out inside every holy word. Today, the peace that rides out on it.
screen: `PRANA.` · `EVERY HOLY WORD RIDES ON IT.`

segments.voice: The Vishnu Purana tells how one school got its strange name. A teacher, Vaishampayana, and his proud student, Yajnavalkya, fall out. The angry teacher says: then give back everything you learned from me. And Yajnavalkya does. He brings up the verses he had learned, right there. The other students take the form of partridges, tittiri, and peck them up. That, the story says, is why their branch of the Veda is called Taittiriya: the partridge school.
screen: `GIVE BACK WHAT YOU LEARNED.` → `PARTRIDGES PECK IT UP.` → `THE PARTRIDGE SCHOOL.`

segments.voice: Now hear the peace chant that opens the second part of the Taittiriya Upanishad, still chanted before study across India. Teacher and student say it together: may God protect us both, may God nourish us both, may we work together with strength, may our study shine, and may we not hate each other. Some teachers hear the story in that line: a school born of a quarrel between teacher and student asks, every time it begins, not to quarrel. Then comes om, shantih, shantih, shantih. Why three times? The traditional explanation is that suffering comes from three directions, so peace is asked three times. Adhyatmika: trouble from within, your own body and mind. Adhibhautika: trouble from other beings, the people and creatures around you. Adhidaivika: trouble from beyond anyone's control, storm and fate and the powers above. Peace within, peace around, peace from beyond. That's why so many Hindu prayers, pujas and readings close this way. And listen to how it ends. Shantih is written with a visarga, an h with a dot under it; in Devanagari, two small dots like a colon. It's a release of breath after the vowel, and reciters often let it carry a faint echo: shanti-hi. Some keep it faint, some let it ring. Om closes with the other mark, anusvara, a hum through the nose. So the chant ends the way it asks: the word is over, and the peace is still breathing out.
screen: `MAY GOD PROTECT US BOTH.` · `MAY WE NOT HATE EACH OTHER.` · `SHANTI: WITHIN, AROUND, BEYOND.` · `VISARGA: SHANTI-HI.` · then, large: `THE PEACE STILL BREATHING.`

segments.voice: If you chant, say om and let the m hum until the breath runs out. Then say shantih three times, slowly, one on each out-breath, letting the visarga carry its soft echo. With the first, think of your own body and mind; with the second, the people and creatures near you; with the third, everything no one controls. If you would rather not chant, say the word peace three times inwardly, with the same three in mind.
Visarga. The breath after the vowel, as in shantiḥ, said shanti-hi: the peace still breathing out.
screen: `VISARGA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: shanti three times: within, around, beyond. One word, three directions. I'll be here tomorrow.

1046.title: Your right is to the work: Gita 2.47
1046.hook: Arjuna drops his bow, and Krishna answers with a line about the work and its fruit
1046.carry: karma yoga: do the work, offer the fruit
1046.tomorrow: would you give up heaven for a dog?
1046.howItsDone: Many Hindus learn Gita 2.47 by heart, and on finishing a task, a meal or a puja quietly say Krishnarpanam astu, "let this be offered to Krishna"; students learn to recite the verses line by line with a teacher, attending to how the words join.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-FORTY-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, shanti three times: peace within, around and beyond, with the visarga still breathing. Today, one real line of the Gita.
screen: `SHANTI: WITHIN, AROUND, BEYOND.` · `THE PEACE STILL BREATHING.`

segments.voice: On the field of Kurukshetra, two armies wait. Arjuna, the finest archer there, asks Krishna, his charioteer, to drive out between them. He looks across and sees his teachers, his cousins, his own grandfather. His bow slips from his hand. He sinks down in the chariot and says: I will not fight. Krishna's answer becomes the Bhagavad Gita, and in its second chapter comes a line millions know by heart: karmaṇy evādhikāras te, mā phaleṣu kadācana.
screen: `ARJUNA DROPS HIS BOW.` → `I WILL NOT FIGHT.` → `KARMAṆY EVĀDHIKĀRAS TE.`

segments.voice: Its sense, in paraphrase: your right is to the work alone, never to its fruits. Don't let the fruit be your motive, and don't cling to doing nothing either. This is the heart of karma yoga, the path of action. Arjuna isn't told to stop caring, or to stop acting. He's told to do what is his to do, fully, and to let go of his grip on how it turns out. A verse later, the Gita calls that evenness yoga. And later still, Krishna takes it one step further: whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you give, do it as an offering to me. That's why many Hindus, finishing a task, a meal or a puja, quietly say Krishnarpanam astu: let this be offered to Krishna. The work is given, and the fruit goes with it. Now hear how the line is built. Karmaṇy: the ṇ curls back. Evādhikāras is two words joined: eva, alone, and adhikāraḥ, right. The two a's merge into a long ā, and the visarga becomes an s because a t comes next. The Taittiriya's old list of the parts of sound calls this kind of thing santana, the joining. Mā phaleṣu: ph is a p that breathes, never an f. Kadācana: c is always ch. Karmaṇy evādhikāras te, mā phaleṣu kadācana. None of this is needed to love the line; the Gita can be held close in any language. But the line makes its own point: say it carefully, as an offering, and let how it sounds to anyone else go.
screen: `YOUR RIGHT IS TO THE WORK.` · `NEVER TO ITS FRUITS.` · `KRISHNARPANAM ASTU: LET IT BE OFFERED.` · `KARMAṆY: THE Ṇ CURLS BACK.` · `EVA + ADHIKĀRAḤ: THE JOINING.` · then, large: `DO THE WORK. OFFER THE FRUIT.`

segments.voice: Say the line one piece per breath: karmaṇy; evādhikāras, holding the long ā; te; mā; phaleṣu, letting the ph breathe; kadācana. Then bring to mind one piece of work whose result you're still waiting on. If you pray, offer it, in words like Krishnarpanam astu, and leave it there. If you don't, simply set it down: your part is done. Sit a few breaths with your hands open.
Santana. The joining: words that lean into each other, as eva and adhikāraḥ do in the Gita's line on the work and its fruit.
screen: `SANTANA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: karma yoga: do the work, offer the fruit. Tomorrow, the year's last block opens on a mountain road. See you then.

1047.title: Yudhishthira's dog
1047.hook: the Mahabharata nears its end on a mountain road, with a dog walking behind a king
1047.carry: dharma: never abandon one who trusts you
1047.tomorrow: what did Yashoda see inside little Krishna's mouth?
1047.howItsDone: The Mahabharata lives in recitations, retellings, plays and television serials; the story of Yudhishthira refusing heaven without the dog is retold as a teaching about loyalty and dharma.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-FORTY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, santana, the joining, and karma yoga: Arjuna's line on the work and its fruit. Today the year's last block begins.
screen: `KARMA YOGA.` · `DO THE WORK. OFFER THE FRUIT.`

segments.voice: Near the end of the Mahabharata, the five Pandava brothers and Draupadi leave their kingdom on foot. A dog falls in behind them and keeps walking. At last they turn north, toward the mountains. On the slope, one walker falls, then another, then another. Yudhishthira, the eldest, keeps going and does not look back. Only the dog is still beside him when a chariot comes down to meet him. This week's days share one name, the summit sit: each climbs back to one stretch of the year and sits there. Today, the great story.
screen: `FIVE BROTHERS, DRAUPADI, AND A DOG.` → `ONE BY ONE, THEY FALL.` → `A WEEK OF SUMMIT SITS.`

segments.voice: The walk has a book of its own inside the epic, the Book of the Great Journey. As each walker falls, Bhima asks his brother why, and Yudhishthira names a cause: a pride, a partiality, an appetite, something each one carried the whole way up. He does not stop to mourn. Then Indra, king of the gods, arrives in his chariot and invites Yudhishthira to rise to heaven in his own body. One condition: the dog stays behind. Yudhishthira refuses. In the story's words, paraphrased: to abandon one who is devoted to you, one who is frightened and has no other refuge, is a grave wrong, and he will not do it, not even for heaven. Indra argues. Yudhishthira holds. And then the dog changes form. It was Dharma himself, the god of righteousness, who in the story is Yudhishthira's own father, testing his son again, as he once did as the Yaksha at the lake. Now see the whole story from up here: the dice game, the forest years, the battlefield and the Gita spoken on it. A story that size could have closed on a war. Near its end it stops instead on a tired man who will not leave a dog on a mountain. That is a teaching the tradition holds high: you do not abandon one who has come to you for refuge, for any reward. Whatever else dharma means across all those books, this test of it is small, and personal, and costs a great deal.
screen: `THE BOOK OF THE GREAT JOURNEY.` · `ONE BY ONE, THE WALKERS FALL.` · `NOT WITHOUT THE DOG.` · `THE DOG WAS DHARMA.` · then, large: `NEVER ABANDON ONE WHO TRUSTS YOU.`

segments.voice: Let the great story walk past you, one figure at a time: Bhishma, Kunti, Karna, Draupadi, Arjuna, Gandhari, Yudhishthira; if one stays, notice who it is, and let that be all right. In the last breaths, bring to mind someone who has walked beside you through a hard stretch of your own road. Just their face.
Dharma. Right conduct, tested once more at the end of the great story, in a king who would not leave a dog on the mountain.
screen: `DHARMA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: dharma: never abandon one who trusts you. Tomorrow, a smaller house, and a child's open mouth. Go gently.

1048.title: The universe in Krishna's mouth
1048.hook: a mother looks into her small son's mouth for dirt and sees everything there is, herself included
1048.carry: vatsalya: loving God as your own child
1048.tomorrow: why didn't the bhakti saints sing in Sanskrit?
1048.howItsDone: The story of Yashoda seeing the universe in Krishna's mouth is told and sung in homes and temples, painted in miniatures, and retold during Janmashtami; devotees speak of vatsalya, loving God as a parent loves a child, and in many homes a small image of the child Krishna (Bal Gopal, Laddu Gopal) is bathed, dressed, fed and rocked.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-FORTY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, dharma at the end of the great story: a king who would not leave a dog on a mountain. Today, a smaller house.
screen: `THE SUMMIT SIT.` · `NOT WITHOUT THE DOG.`

segments.voice: The other boys come running to Yashoda with a complaint: Krishna has been eating dirt. She grabs his hand and scolds him. He looks up, all innocence, and says they're lying. If she doesn't believe him, she can look for herself. So she does the obvious thing. Open your mouth, she says. He opens it. And she does not find dirt.
screen: `HE'S BEEN EATING DIRT.` → `OPEN YOUR MOUTH.` → `NO DIRT.`

segments.voice: Here is what the Bhagavata Purana says she saw, in paraphrase. Inside the little mouth: the sky in every direction, the mountains, the islands and oceans, the earth, wind and fire, the moon and the stars. The whole moving world. And inside all of that, the village of Vraja. And inside the village, herself, standing there, looking into a child's mouth. Yashoda is shaken. The text lets her wonder aloud: is this a dream? A trick of the gods' illusion? Some power in my own boy? She bows, in her heart, to the one who holds all of it. Then comes the turn. The text says Krishna spread his maya over her, his power of veiling, in the form of a mother's love. She forgets what she has seen. She lifts him onto her lap, and he is her son again, a boy who may or may not have eaten dirt. Again and again the Krishna stories hold two things at once. The child is the whole universe. The child is also just a child who needs his face washed. Some readers hear Yashoda's forgetting as a gift, not a loss: the ordinary love handed back. That love has a name in bhakti: vatsalya, loving God the way a parent loves a child. And it is a real way of worship. In many Hindu homes a small image of the child Krishna, Bal Gopal or Laddu Gopal, is bathed, dressed, fed and put to rest, and at Janmashtami his cradle is rocked. God, who holds the universe, is let in as someone small to care for.

segments.voice: Let this be a sit in two halves. First, widen: let attention open past the room, to the sky and everything under it, the way Yashoda saw it all at once. Then, halfway, come home. If you pray, picture the child Krishna, or the form of God you love, as small and near, and offer him something in your mind: a sip of water, a sweet, a blanket. If you don't, bring to mind a child you have cared for, and stay with that tenderness.
Vatsalya. Tender parental love, the veil that let Yashoda hold her son again after she saw the whole universe in his mouth.

1049.title: Bhakti in the language of home
1049.hook: a weaver, a tailor, a shopkeeper and a princess, all singing to God in the language of home
1049.carry: bhakti: God hears love in any language
1049.tomorrow: what did Ramana ask himself at sixteen?
1049.howItsDone: The songs of the bhakti saints are sung in homes, temples and on pilgrim walks across India: Tukaram's abhangas, Kabir's dohas, Mirabai's bhajans and Andal's Tiruppavai, each in its own language.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-FORTY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, vatsalya: Yashoda saw the universe in her son's mouth, and a mother's love gave her back her son. Today, the singers.
screen: `THE SUMMIT SIT.` · `VAST, AND SMALL, AT ONCE.`

segments.voice: A weaver at his loom in Varanasi, throwing the shuttle and singing. A tailor in Maharashtra with a needle in his hand and a name of God on his lips. A shopkeeper whose ledgers of money owed to him, the story goes, ended up in the river. A princess in Rajasthan who sang that she had no one but Krishna. A girl in a Tamil temple town who wore the garland meant for the god before it was offered. Faces from the weeks of the saints of bhakti.
screen: `A WEAVER, A TAILOR, A SHOPKEEPER.` → `A PRINCESS, A GARDEN GIRL.` → `THE SAINTS OF BHAKTI.`

segments.voice: From the top of the year, look at who the tradition chose to remember. Kabir is remembered as a weaver. Namdev as a tailor. Tukaram as a small trader whose business failed. Mirabai as a princess who walked away from palace rules. Andal as a girl raised by a temple gardener. Looms, needles, ledgers, a palace, a garden. And notice what they sang in. Andal and the Nayanars sang in Tamil. Jnaneshwar, Namdev and Tukaram in Marathi. Kabir, Surdas, Tulsidas and Mirabai in the spoken tongues of the north. In Bengal, the songs of Chaitanya's kirtan were made in Bengali. The language of the kitchen and the market became a language of prayer. A song credited to Kabir lets God speak, in paraphrase: where are you looking for me? I am right beside you. Not in the temple, not in the mosque, not in ritual and renunciation. Seek truly and you will find me in a moment. Mirabai, in paraphrase: my own is Giridhar Gopal, the cowherd who lifted the mountain, and no one else. Different saints, different gods named, different tongues. One shared teaching, and it is the heart of bhakti: God is reached by love, and love doesn't need the priest's language. Sanskrit stays sacred; it was never the only door. That's why songs from those weeks are still sung by heart in kitchens, on pilgrim roads and in temple halls, in the language each family speaks.
screen: `REMEMBERED BY THEIR TRADES.` · `SUNG IN THE LANGUAGE OF HOME.` · `I AM RIGHT BESIDE YOU.` · `NO ONE ELSE BUT GIRIDHAR GOPAL.` · then, large: `GOD HEARS LOVE IN ANY LANGUAGE.`

segments.voice: Find the language you first heard tenderness in, whatever it is. If you pray, let one name of God in that language rest on the breath, again and again, the way the saints repeated a name; if you don't, choose a plain word for thanks in that same tongue. Let it come and go with the breath, like a weaver's shuttle, back and forth.
Bhakti. Loving devotion, the saints' whole path, sung to God in the language of home.

1050.title: Ramana at sixteen: who am I?
1050.hook: a sixteen-year-old lies down on the floor as if dead, and asks what dies
1050.carry: atman: the one the thoughts come to
1050.tomorrow: how can someone work in the world and not get stained?
1050.howItsDone: People who follow Ramana Maharshi's teaching practice self-inquiry by asking "who am I?" whenever thoughts arise, in sitting practice and in daily life, and many visit his ashram at Arunachala in Tiruvannamalai; Vivekananda's addresses and Tagore's Gitanjali are read and recited widely.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-FIFTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, bhakti: the saints who sang to God in the language of home. Today, the modern teachers.
screen: `BHAKTI.` · `GOD HEARS LOVE IN ANY LANGUAGE.`

segments.voice: Madurai, in south India, 1896. A schoolboy of sixteen named Venkataraman is alone in an upstairs room of his uncle's house. He isn't ill. But, as he later told it, a sudden, overwhelming fear of death comes over him. He doesn't run for help. He lies down, stretches out stiff like a corpse, holds his breath, and asks himself: this body is dead. They'll carry it to the burning ground. But am I dead?
screen: `MADURAI, 1896. A BOY OF SIXTEEN.` → `HE LIES DOWN AS IF DEAD.` → `BUT AM I DEAD?`

segments.voice: His answer, as he later told it, didn't come as an argument. The body lay still, and he felt himself fully alive, untouched by its death. About six weeks later he left home for the holy hill of Arunachala, at Tiruvannamalai, and he stayed there the rest of his life. People came from everywhere to sit with him, and called him Ramana Maharshi. His teaching was the question that boy asked on the floor: who am I? It is one of the oldest teachings in Hinduism, made small enough to carry. The Upanishads call it atman: the Self, the one who sees, which is not the body and not the thoughts. In Advaita Vedanta, the school Ramana's teaching is usually placed in, atman is one with Brahman. His short text Who Am I? turns it into a practice, self-inquiry. Thoughts will keep coming. Don't chase them, and don't fight them. When one arrives, ask: to whom has this come? To me. Then: who am I? The mind, he says, turns back toward its source, and the thought falls quiet. In the end the questioning itself burns up, like the stick used to stir a funeral fire. The question isn't a riddle with an answer like I am this body. It turns attention around, from what appears to the one it appears to. The other modern teachers carried old paths into new rooms too: Vivekananda opened in Chicago with "Sisters and Brothers of America"; Gandhi read the Gita as a guide to action; Tagore made prayer into Gitanjali. Ramana carried it into one question.
screen: `FULLY ALIVE. THEN, ARUNACHALA.` · `WHO AM I? ATMAN: THE SELF.` · `THOUGHTS COME. ASK: TO WHOM?` · `TO ME. WHO AM I?` · then, large: `TURN ATTENTION AROUND.`

segments.voice: Let the breath settle, and when a thought arrives, neither follow it nor push it away; ask quietly, to whom did this come? To me. Then ask, who am I? Don't answer in words: let attention turn back toward the one who is asking, and rest there until the next thought comes.
Ramana. The boy of sixteen who asked what dies, and whose whole path fits in one question: who am I?

segments.voice: Your line: atman: the one the thoughts come to. Tomorrow, a lotus leaf. Back tomorrow, same hill.
